gist: Lawfare panel (despite the 'Techs Appeal' title, tech/AI appears only in opening banter about Trump rebranding AI as 'SI') covers the Supreme Court's third grant of permission for third-country deportations with an unusual one-sided invitation to the government, the likely survival of Judge Boasberg's contempt inquiry, the dismantling of DOJ/FBI public-corruption units that killed a Susan Collins bribery probe, counterintelligence risks around Trump-circle weddings, and the White House press bans plus taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads.

insights.claim: For the third time, the Supreme Court stayed a lower-court block and allowed the Trump administration to keep deporting migrants to third countries with no connection to them, while granting cert with oral argument set for December 2026.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Third-country removal policy stays operative at least until a merits ruling in 2027.
insights.quote: the Supreme Court again has allowed third country removals to continue at least for the next few months temporarily

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's one-paragraph order unusually invited only the government to add any other questions presented it deems relevant, which panelists say tilts the adversarial playing field toward the executive.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Signals a merits ruling could sweep broader than the narrow issue litigated below, favoring executive immigration power.
insights.quote: I've never seen that sort of direction in a court order to a single party.

insights.claim: The open-ended invitation could bring in issues never briefed in lower courts, depriving the Court of the fact-intensive lower-court analysis it conventionally relies on; respondents are expected to push for advance notice of the government's added topics.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Expect procedural skirmishing over the scope of the December argument before briefing.

insights.claim: The approach aligns with Justice Kavanaugh's stated view that the Court should decide recurring emergency issues definitively to provide clarity rather than tiptoe around binding precedent.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Kavanaugh's efficiency rationale may drive more expansive shadow-to-merits conversions.

insights.claim: Class counsel recently had to file an emergency motion after learning of a planned deportation flight to the Central African Republic and Burundi, countries carrying the highest State Department travel advisory levels.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Illustrates the conduct of the party the Court is advantaging.

insights.claim: The administration flew Somali men held at Guantanamo Bay to Mogadishu hours after an appeals court made clear the third-country removal policy was blocked, after telling them the plane was only stopping in Cuba to refuel.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Pattern of racing removals ahead of or despite court orders.

insights.claim: If justices like Kavanaugh are upset that lower courts misapply shadow-docket rulings, the fix is entirely within their control: explain their reasoning, since hundreds of lower courts otherwise must guess.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Unexplained emergency orders structurally generate inconsistent lower-court outcomes.
insights.quote: that is a problem that is entirely within their own control to solve

themes.theme: Boasberg contempt inquiry and court compliance

insights.claim: The en banc D.C. Circuit appears likely to let Judge Boasberg proceed in some form with his contempt inquiry over the 2025 Alien Enemies Act flights to El Salvador, because a majority recognizes the government's position would leave district courts unable to police compliance.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Contempt inquiry likely survives, building an evidentiary record on executive defiance.
insights.quote: the onbanc court is likely to allow Judge Boseberg to proceed with this inquiry in some fashion

insights.claim: The government's position is that once it names the responsible decision-maker, a district court can do nothing more than refer for prosecution, which would be handled by the executive branch itself.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Accepting this would make judicial contempt power against the executive largely toothless.

insights.claim: The government named Kristi Noem, who is no longer in government, as the decision-maker who sent the planes on, which some see as offering a sacrificial lamb.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Shifting accountability to departed officials limits contempt exposure.

insights.claim: Judges Katsas, Rao and Walker were more skeptical of the inquiry, with possible hooks including that Boasberg's written order superseded his oral order and was ambiguous about whether 'removal' meant from US custody or US territory.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: These narrower arguments are the likely path if the case reaches the Supreme Court.

insights.claim: Judge Katsas is a good proxy for the center of the Supreme Court, so his minority view may be more persuasive to Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett if the case goes up.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Watch Katsas's opinion as a leading indicator of the Supreme Court outcome.
insights.quote: I think Judge Katsis is a good metric for kind of where the center of the Supreme Court would be.

insights.claim: Even if the inquiry proceeds, the government will likely throw further obstacles such as attorney-client or executive privilege to block testimony, so more appeals are expected.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Contempt accountability timeline will stretch out considerably.

insights.claim: The easiest relief to obtain is permission to build the evidentiary record; actual contempt findings and referral standards are harder and can be reviewed later.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Near-term wins for courts will be investigative, not punitive.

insights.claim: Judges, including some Trump appointees, are increasingly holding or threatening to hold DHS and DOJ officials in contempt for violating court orders in deportation cases.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Executive-judicial confrontation is broadening beyond a single case.

insights.claim: Courts' usual strategy of pressuring the administration by entertaining sanctions becomes much dicier against an administration consciously practicing brinkmanship until it meets hard institutional pushback; the open question is when Roberts or Barrett will embrace tougher remedies.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: The swing justices' tolerance is the key variable in whether courts ultimately enforce orders.

insights.claim: Many compliance failures arise from routine district-court immigration orders the government simply ignores, not from ambiguity created by shadow-docket rulings.
insights.speaker: Anna Bower
insights.so_what: Non-compliance is a behavioral, not doctrinal, problem.

insights.claim: By late 2024 FBI agents believed they had enough evidence to seek a sweeping bribery probe tied to a defense contractor's illegal donations to Sen. Susan Collins and others, but it died when the administration gutted the relevant FBI and DOJ units.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Becomes a live issue in Collins's tight re-election race.

insights.claim: DOJ's Public Integrity Section has been functionally if not officially disbanded, with almost all staff reassigned or fired, largely after the Eric Adams case-dismissal episode and because Jack Smith had drawn on it.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Federal capacity to prosecute public officials is largely gone.
insights.quote: The units whose very existence is to help move these sort of cases forward just don't exist anymore.

insights.claim: Kash Patel disbanded the FBI Washington Field Office squad that ran both the Collins probe and the Arctic Frost election investigation, leaving the capital's field office without a public corruption squad for a significant period.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Corruption cases involving officials in DC face no dedicated investigators.

insights.claim: Dropping a case against a Republican senator whose seat is needed to hold the Senate majority does not pass the smell test, and observers should expect more such cases to die because the investigators are gone.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Expect reduced deterrence against bribery and access-buying.
insights.quote: if you're outraged with this sort of case getting dropped, just get used to it

insights.claim: No one at the FBI, DOJ or Tom Homan himself has denied reports that he accepted a bag of cash, allegedly captured on video or audio; they only say no crime occurred.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Non-denials suggest the underlying facts are accurate.

insights.claim: Successive dropped cases (Homan, Adams, Collins) produce public desensitization, each bombshell landing with less sting, which shifts the Overton window on corruption.
insights.speaker: Tyler McBrien
insights.so_what: Political cost of corruption revelations is declining.

themes.theme: Access-buying and counterintelligence risk around Trump circle

insights.claim: A Putin-linked Russian oligarch reportedly underwrote millions for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding events, which sits where public corruption and counterintelligence concerns overlap because Trump Jr. holds over $600 million in defense contracts.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Defense-contracting ties of the president's family create foreign leverage risk.
insights.quote: the part of the ven diagram where public corruption and counterintelligence concerns overlap

insights.claim: Wedding guests like Jared Kushner, though not government employees, conduct some of the most sensitive US diplomacy, magnifying the risk of gifts from a country tied to a great-power rival in a proxy war in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Informal diplomats are exposed to foreign influence without official ethics constraints.

insights.claim: Trump said he would tell his son to pay the money back, which Feinberg argues is an implicit admission that accepting it was inappropriate.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Repayment pledges validate the impropriety concern.

insights.claim: At Alina Habba's wedding, attended by FBI Director Kash Patel and Todd Blanche, guests included a man photographed with Habba and Patel whom the FBI had recommended for deportation because, while allegedly an FBI source, he was working for a foreign country.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Senior law-enforcement officials mixing with suspected foreign agents is a counterintelligence red flag.

themes.theme: White House media war and taxpayer-funded ads

insights.claim: The White House banned CNN, MS Now and Politico and had the Secret Service seize press passes; a federal judge temporarily restored access, finding the ban likely violated due process.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Courts remain a check on press access restrictions.

insights.claim: The press-ban idea was reportedly fueled by aide Natalie Harp showing Trump unfavorable coverage, reflecting a last-person-in-the-room influence dynamic.
insights.speaker: Tyler McBrien
insights.so_what: Policy can be driven by idiosyncratic personal grievances of whoever has access.

insights.claim: Taxpayer-funded White House ads closely track Trump campaign messaging, one nearly identical to a 2024 spot, weeks before the midterms, and the 'he's not on the ballot' defense rings hollow since Trump urges crowds to act as if he is.
insights.speaker: Tyler McBrien
insights.so_what: Legal and political exposure around use of public funds for campaign-style messaging.

insights.claim: Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other Republicans publicly said taxpayer money shouldn't fund the ads, signaling strain between the administration and congressional allies who don't want Trump appearing for them.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: GOP midterm candidates are distancing from an unpopular president.

insights.claim: Trump is more unpopular than George W. Bush was in 2006, driven by a perception that personal interests drive his decisions; a Reuters poll found 69% of Americans hold that view, including about two-thirds of independents.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Midterm headwinds for Republicans in competitive districts.

insights.claim: The public tends to overlook rule-of-law issues until they hit their pocketbook, so the taxpayer-funded ads are unlikely to provoke much reaction outside the Beltway.
insights.speaker: Mike Feinberg
insights.so_what: Don't expect voter backlash on norms issues absent economic pain.
insights.quote: they're sort of willing to look the other way until it hits them in the pocketbook

insights.claim: A media operation staffed with true-believing internet trolls produces messaging that delights a base already voting for you without expanding support, making the ads an expensive scrap of meat for the base.
insights.speaker: Scott R. Anderson
insights.so_what: Administration communications are optimized for base engagement, not persuasion.
